:::{#thm-orthonormal-expansion}
#### Coordinates in an orthonormal basis are dot products

If $\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_k$ is an orthonormal basis of a subspace $\mathcal{S}$
(@def-orthonormal-basis), then every $\vecf{x} \in \mathcal{S}$ satisfies

$$
\vecf{x} = \sumto{i}{k} (\vecf{q}_i \cdot \vecf{x})\,\vecf{q}_i.
$$

:::

::: proof

The basis spans $\mathcal{S}$,
so $\vecf{x} = \sumto{j}{k} c_j \vecf{q}_j$ for some numbers $c_j$.
For each $i$,

$$
\ba
\vecf{q}_i \cdot \vecf{x}
&= \vecf{q}_i \cdot \paren{\sumto{j}{k} c_j \vecf{q}_j}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \sumto{j}{k} c_j\,(\vecf{q}_i \cdot \vecf{q}_j)
&& \text{(@thm-dot-linear-sum)}
\\
&= c_i,
&& \text{(@def-orthonormal-vectors)}
\ea
$$

so each coefficient $c_i$ is $\vecf{q}_i \cdot \vecf{x}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-orthonormal-expansion}
#### Expanding a vector in an orthonormal basis

With the orthonormal basis $\vecf{q}_1, \vecf{q}_2, \vecf{q}_3$ of $\reals^3$
from @exm-orthonormal-basis and $\vecf{x} = (1, 2, 3)$:
$\vecf{q}_1 \cdot \vecf{x} = 3$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vecf{q}_2 \cdot \vecf{x} &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,(1 + 2) \\
&= \tfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vecf{q}_3 \cdot \vecf{x} &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,(1 - 2) \\
&= -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\ba
\sumto{i}{3} (\vecf{q}_i \cdot \vecf{x})\,\vecf{q}_i
&= 3\,(0, 0, 1) + \tfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,(1, 1, 0)
 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,(1, -1, 0)
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= (0, 0, 3) + \paren{\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}, 0} + \paren{-\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}, 0}
&& \text{(multiply out each term)}
\\
&= (1, 2, 3),
&& \text{(add entrywise)}
\ea
$$

which is $\vecf{x}$, as @thm-orthonormal-expansion says.

:::
